title: Beyond Good and Evil
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
length: 9 parts, aphorisms 1–296 with three supplements, and a closing poem
openingText: Supposing that Truth is a woman — what then? Is there not ground for suspecting that all philosophers, insofar as they have been dogmatists, have failed to understand women — that the terrible seriousness and clumsy importunity with which they have usually paid their addresses to Truth have been unskilled and unseemly methods for winning a woman? Certainly she has never allowed herself to be won; and at present every kind of dogma stands with a sad and discouraged mien — if, indeed, it stands at all! There are scoffers who maintain that it has fallen, that all dogma lies on the ground — nay more, that it is at its last gasp. But to speak seriously, there are good grounds for hoping that all dogmatizing in philosophy — whatever solemn, whatever conclusive and decided airs it has assumed — may have been only a noble childishness and novice work; and probably the time is at hand when it will be understood once and again what has actually sufficed for the foundation of such imposing and absolute philosophical edifices as the dogmatists have hitherto reared. Perhaps some popular superstition of immemorial time (such as the soul-superstition, which in the form of subject- and ego-superstition has not yet ceased doing mischief); perhaps some play upon words, a deception on the part of grammar, or an audacious generalization of very restricted, very personal, very human — all-too-human — facts. The dogmatists' philosophy, it is to be hoped, was only a promise for thousands of years afterwards, as astrology was in still earlier times, in whose service probably more labor, money, acuteness, and patience have been spent than on any actual science hitherto: we owe to it, and to its "super-terrestrial" pretensions in Asia and Egypt, the grand style of architecture. It seems that in order to inscribe themselves on the heart of humanity with everlasting claims, all great things must first wander about the earth as enormous and awe-inspiring caricatures. Dogmatic philosophy has been a caricature of this kind — for instance, the Vedanta doctrine in Asia, and Platonism in Europe. Let us not be ungrateful to it, though it must be confessed that the worst, the most long-lasting, and the most dangerous of errors hitherto has been a dogmatist error — namely, Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself. But now that it has been overcome, now that Europe, rid of this nightmare, can again draw breath freely and at least enjoy a healthier sleep, we whose very duty is wakefulness are the heirs of all the strength that the struggle against this error has fostered. It amounted to the very inversion of truth and the denial of perspective — the fundamental condition of life — to speak of Spirit and the Good as Plato spoke of them. One might indeed ask, like a physician: "How did such a malady attack that finest product of antiquity, Plato? Had the wicked Socrates really corrupted him? Was Socrates after all a corrupter of youths, and did he deserve his hemlock?" But the struggle against Plato — or, to speak more plainly and for "the people," the struggle against millennia of ecclesiastical oppression by Christianity (for Christianity is Platonism for "the people") — produced in Europe a magnificent tension of spirit such as had not existed anywhere previously. With such a tensely strained bow one can now aim at the furthest goals. Of course the European feels this tension as a state of distress, and twice grand attempts have been made to unbend the bow: once by means of Jesuitism, the second time by means of democratic enlightenment — which, with the aid of freedom of the press and newspaper-reading, might indeed bring it about that the spirit no longer so easily finds itself in "distress"! (The Germans invented gunpowder — all credit to them! but they then made things square — they invented printing.) But we, who are neither Jesuits nor democrats nor even sufficiently Germans — we good Europeans and free, very free spirits — we still have it: all the distress of spirit and all the tension of its bow! And perhaps also the arrow, the task, and — who knows? — the goal.
about: Why would a philosopher want truth at any price? Nietzsche turns the question back on philosophers themselves. Across nine parts he moves between extended arguments, sharp asides, and imagined conversations. He reads moral judgments for what they reveal about the people making them and asks who might dare to create new values. The book appeared in 1886 with the subtitle “Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future.”

angleCards.title: Read the philosopher between the lines
angleCards.text: In § 6 Nietzsche calls great philosophy a kind of involuntary memoir. What desires might a thinker reveal precisely when he thinks he is speaking impersonally?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read an argument for what it reveals about the person making it.

angleCards.title: Try out a thought
angleCards.text: Watch the conditionals in § 36. Nietzsche puts the will to power to the test. How far does the experiment go, and what does he ask us to assume?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish what Nietzsche asserts from what he asks me to imagine.

angleCards.title: Compare ways of judging
angleCards.text: In § 260 Nietzsche distinguishes master morality from slave morality. The two can coexist in one person. Watch how the word “good” changes its meaning.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to see how different experiences give the same word a different weight.

angleCards.title: Listen for a change of voice
angleCards.text: An argument can turn into a joke. The book ends with a poem about a host waiting for friends. What can the poem say that the argument cannot?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the rhythm, the irony, and the shifts between voices.

cast.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
cast.description: He speaks by turns as a psychologist, an opponent, and someone trying out a thought. Pay attention to whom he addresses.

cast.name: Master morality
cast.description: In § 260 the noble person first calls something good out of a sense of personal worth. Only then does the contrast with what is judged inferior arise.

cast.name: Slave morality
cast.description: In Nietzsche’s account, helpfulness, patience, and kindness take on particular value for people who must live under the power of others.

cast.name: The will to power
cast.description: In § 36 Nietzsche asks whether the forces of the world might be understood through our experience of drives and willing.

cast.name: The free spirit
cast.description: Breaking with an old conviction is one thing. Recognizing what binds you now is another.

cast.name: Plato and Schopenhauer
cast.description: Plato’s conception of the good and Schopenhauer’s account of the will give Nietzsche occasions to examine the assumptions his predecessors made.

whyItMatters.title: What is truth worth?
whyItMatters.body: In § 1 the question shifts: why do we want truth more than uncertainty? Even the wish for a certain answer becomes something to investigate.

whyItMatters.title: Whose morality?
whyItMatters.body: In § 186 Nietzsche calls for descriptions and comparisons of different moralities. Otherwise a philosopher may simply justify the values already familiar to him.

whyItMatters.title: When the reader objects
whyItMatters.body: Nietzsche’s remarks on women, rank, and obedience invite a reader to turn his own questions back on him: whose experiences and desires are finding a voice here?
